content.title: About
content.content: Collards (Brassica oleracea var. acephala) are leafy vegetables from the cruciferous family, cultivated in North Carolina (NS). When cooked they retain a bright green color, tender texture and a mildly bitter flavor. They are a staple in Southern cuisine, used in soups, stews and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Collards belong to the same species as cabbage, broccoli and kale.
Traditionally in the Southern United States they are cooked with smoked meat or sausage.
The leaves are rich in chlorophyll, giving them a deep green hue.
In the US they are often called “Southern kale”.
Collard seeds can be sprouted, though culinary use focuses on the leaves.

items.title: High in vitamins K and C
items.content: A 100‑g serving of cooked collard greens provides over 800 % of the daily value for vitamin K and about 30 % of vitamin C, supporting blood clotting and immune function.

items.title: Rich source of fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports bone health
items.content: Calcium and magnesium contribute to strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: One cup of cooked collard greens contains roughly 30 kcal, making it an excellent choice for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Thyroid considerations
items.content: Cruciferous vegetables contain goitrogens that, in very large amounts, may affect thyroid function.

items.title: Food‑drug interactions
items.content: High vitamin K intake can reduce the effectiveness of anticoagulants such as warfarin.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to cruciferous vegetables.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook collard greens by boiling or steaming for 5‑10 minutes until tender. They can be served as a side, added to soups, stews, or braised with meat. Before cooking, rinse thoroughly and remove tough stems.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh leaves keep in the refrigerator in a perforated bag for up to 5 days. Cooked greens should be stored in an airtight container in the fridge and consumed within 3 days.
